clinicalPearls: Caries is a chronic, biofilm-mediated disease driven by repeated acid production from fermentable carbohydrates, not a simple one-off infection
Early lesions appear as chalky white spots that represent subsurface demineralisation and can still remineralise before cavitation occurs
Pit-and-fissure surfaces, interproximal contacts, and exposed root surfaces in older patients are the sites most prone to decay
Symptoms often lag behind disease; sensitivity to sweet, cold, or hot stimuli suggests progression toward the pulp
Bitewing radiographs are key for detecting interproximal lesions that are hidden on visual examination
Management balances remineralisation strategies (fluoride, diet control, oral hygiene) for early lesions against operative restoration once cavitation is established
High caries risk should prompt assessment of salivary flow, diet, fluoride exposure, and plaque control rather than only drilling and filling
Untreated caries is the usual precursor to pulpitis, periapical infection, and eventual tooth loss
reference.pathophysiology: Dental caries results from an ecological shift in the dental plaque biofilm favouring acidogenic and aciduric bacteria such as mutans streptococci and lactobacilli. Frequent intake of fermentable sugars fuels bacterial acid production, lowering plaque pH below the critical threshold and driving demineralisation of enamel hydroxyapatite. When acid attacks outpace the buffering and remineralising capacity of saliva and fluoride, subsurface mineral loss progresses to surface cavitation. The lesion then advances through dentine, where tubular structure allows faster spread, ultimately reaching and infecting the pulp if untreated.
additionalDifferentials: Dental erosion from intrinsic or extrinsic acids
Fluorosis or intrinsic staining mimicking lesions
additionalInvestigations: Visual-tactile examination with good lighting and drying of surfaces
Bitewing and periapical radiographs for interproximal and root lesions
Caries risk assessment including diet and salivary evaluation
Pulp sensibility testing when pulpal involvement is suspected
Adjunctive detection methods (transillumination, laser fluorescence) where available
redFlags: Spreading facial swelling, fever, or trismus indicating odontogenic infection extending beyond the tooth
Rampant or early childhood caries suggesting major dietary or salivary dysfunction
Signs of pulpal necrosis or periapical involvement requiring urgent endodontic assessment
reference.prognosis: Early non-cavitated lesions can be arrested or reversed with preventive measures, while cavitated lesions require restoration but carry a good prognosis when risk factors are controlled; neglected disease progresses to pulpitis, abscess, and tooth loss.
pitfalls: Restoring cavities without addressing underlying diet and hygiene, leading to recurrent decay
Overlooking interproximal or hidden root-surface lesions on clinical inspection alone
Mistaking arrested or remineralised lesions for active disease and over-treating
Ignoring salivary hypofunction as a driver of rapid caries progression
